title: Our Neighbours Have Gone
intro: This is one of Jarir's well-known poems, a satire on al-Akhtal, the poet of Taghlib, from the long exchange of verse insults between the two. Its love prelude is the most famous part: Ibn Qutayba quotes its opening and its line on the eyes among his examples of verse whose words are beautiful and sweet though there is little meaning beneath them. It begins with the beloved's people moving away and a greeting to their old camp. The poet sends his greetings with a rider to the people of the Ghawr and speaks to his beloved under several names, Umm Amr, Tayba and Umm Uthman, complaining of her coldness and her broken faith and counting the places where love nearly killed him. He describes eyes that kill and never bring their dead to life, her phantom visiting him in sleep, the departing litters, the camels wearing their feet raw on the road, and his longing for Mount al-Rayyan, the south wind and the days of his youth. At the end the poem turns to boasting and threats: he warns the poets who wished to take him on, and boasts of his standing among Khindif and Qays Aylan. The recitation stops at that boast, leaving out the closing lines of abuse against al-Akhtal and Taghlib.

translation: The neighbours have gone; had I been obeyed, they would not have gone,
and they have cut the cords of our union, strand by strand.
1.sharh: The poem opens, as the old odes do, with the beloved's people breaking camp and moving on. Union is a rope, and they have cut it.

translation: Greet the dwellings, from the days when we wanted no other
home than that home, and no other neighbours than those.
2.sharh: Greet the camp where we once lived, when none of us wanted any other home or other neighbours. The greeting goes to the place for the sake of the time: the old ode stops at the ruins to remember a contentment that is gone.

translation: I followed the departing litters, shaken,
afraid of parting, and full of grief.
3.sharh: He followed the litters with his eyes, shaken and afraid of the parting before it came.

translation: How many a sad man, were my death announced to him,
would weep, and another would be glad of the news.
4.sharh: Some would weep at the news of his death and others rejoice. He has his mourners and his enemies alike, and the glad listener is a first hint of the satire with which the poem ends.

translation: If you knew what we suffer, you would pity us,
or if you heard our complaint to the Lord of the Throne,
5.sharh: If she knew what he suffers she would pity him, or if she could hear him complaining of it to God. He takes his complaint over her head, to the Lord of the Throne, and the next line shows how desperately.

translation: like a man at sea whose ship heels over in the waves,
calling on God in secret and aloud.
6.sharh: His prayer is that of a sailor whose ship heels over in a storm, crying to God under his breath and out loud. The lover in his distress is a man about to go under.

translation: You rider, urging on your mount,
carry our greeting, and may God grant you a mount to ride,
7.sharh: The rider who carries a lover's message is a stock figure of the old ode; the blessing is a traveller's wish.

translation: carry messages from us, light to bear,
on young she-camels that have never foaled,
8.sharh: Carry our messages: words weigh nothing, and the mounts are young she-camels that have never foaled, the swiftest and strongest. The message is light, and he wants it carried fast.

translation: so that we may say, when you have done our errand:
“You are the trustworthy one, when the trusted betray.”
9.sharh: Do our errand, and we will call you the one trustworthy man in a world where the trusted betray: he spurs the rider on with the praise he will earn.

translation: You bring greetings to the people of the Ghawr from Malah:
how far from Malah is the Ghawr where they are taken.
10.sharh: The rider is to take greetings from Malah to the Ghawr, and the poet marvels at the distance between them. Longing crosses distances that meeting cannot.

translation: How dear to me a camp by that bend of the valley,
its acacias above all acacias, its camel-pens above all pens.
11.sharh: He loves the place down to its trees and its watering pens because she camped there.

translation: If only this heart might meet someone to console it,
or a cupbearer to give it, today, the draught of forgetting,
12.sharh: He wants to forget and cannot; “if only” is the wish of a man who knows it will not come.

translation: or if only she had never bound us with her love,
and that love had never entered in as it did.
13.sharh: He wishes he had never known her at all, the last word in a lover's complaint.

translation: Will you not fear the sin of what you do to us,
you whose sleeves are the sweetest of all on a rainy day?
14.sharh: A day of cloud and rain was a day spent indoors, when perfume hangs in the air.

translation: She said, “Call on us, if you are leaving:
I do not think you will meet us after today.”
15.sharh: She asks him to call on them before he leaves, since she does not expect to see him again. It is the last visit before the parting, and her words make the parting final.

translation: Tayba, have you any gift to give
a guest who came to you at dawn, Tayba, in haste?
16.sharh: He is a guest on the point of leaving, asking for something to take with him.

translation: I was not the first to long and to be shaken,
whose griefs were stirred by mornings of parting.
17.sharh: Others before him have longed and been shaken, their grief stirred by the mornings when the tribe broke camp. He consoles himself: parting is every lover's lot.

translation: Umm Amr, may God reward you with forgiveness:
give me back my heart as it used to be.
18.sharh: He prays that God forgive Umm Amr, and asks her to give him back his heart as it was before he loved her. It is in her keeping, and only she can return it.

translation: Are you not the fairest of all who walk on foot,
you whose eyes are the loveliest of all mankind's?
19.sharh: He praises all of her, then her eyes above all, and the repeated “people” makes her the loveliest of everyone.

translation: Whoever has a claim on you, though you are not in want,
meets with meanness for generosity, denial for kindness.
20.sharh: Like a debtor who could pay and will not, she withholds the love she owes him.

translation: Never feel safe, as I do not,
from the treachery of a friend who shows many colours.
21.sharh: He warns, from his own experience, never to feel safe from a friend who keeps changing colour: whoever shows many colours will in the end betray.

translation: You have betrayed one who never feared your betrayal;
you are not the first trusted one to betray.
22.sharh: She has betrayed a man who never feared she would; but she is not the first trusted one to betray. He reproaches her, and in the same breath makes light of it, as if betrayal were only to be expected.

translation: I hid my love until it took my wits away;
I can hide this love no longer.
23.sharh: He kept his love hidden as long as he could, until it overwhelmed his reason; now it is beyond hiding. Concealment lasted until love grew stronger than he was.

translation: Love nearly killed me on the day of Sulmanayn,
and nearly killed me one day at Baydan,
24.sharh: Love nearly killed him at Sulmanayn and again at Baydan. He counts love's battles by place-names, as a warrior counts the days of his combats.

translation: and nearly killed me on the day of Liwa Hawwa',
had I been a stranger to the sighs of parting.
25.sharh: Only his long experience of partings saved him; a man untouched by them would have died.

translation: May God withhold His blessing from whoever thought you
nothing but true to your word, until what happened happened.
26.sharh: He curses whoever thought she would keep her word, until she broke it. That man is himself: he curses his own trust in her.

translation: So great is my love for you, know that love has its station:
I love your guardian, if only he loved me.
27.sharh: Love spreads from the beloved to whoever is close to her, even the man who guards her.

translation: May God not bless the world if the cords
of your world are cut from the cords of mine.
28.sharh: Let the world be cursed if her life and his are cut apart. His world means nothing unless its cords are joined to hers.

translation: Umm Uthman, love comes by chance:
it leads the wise astray, and at times it makes the eye weep.
29.sharh: Love comes unsought, he tells Umm Uthman: it turns the wisest man into a boy and sometimes makes the eye weep. Love is not chosen, and it overcomes the most level-headed.

translation: She has refused us a watering place once open to us,
that quenched the thirst of the love-crazed, thirsting heart.
30.sharh: She now denies him the watering place that was once open to him, whose water cured the thirst of a heart lost in love. Her love was water, and her refusal leaves him parched.

translation: How can we meet, when your summer camp
is not near ours, nor your spring pasture ours?
31.sharh: Desert tribes gathered at wells in summer and scattered to pasture in spring; their two tribes meet at neither.

translation: We love the soil of al-Irq, for since you left we have found
no valley like al-Irq, no al-Sullan like al-Sullan.
32.sharh: Since she left he has found no valley like al-Irq or al-Sullan, so he loves their very soil. The places are dear because they used to meet there.

translation: Time has worked no change in me, as you know,
no cutting of the cord, no forgetting of the pledge.
33.sharh: Nothing time has brought, as she well knows, has made him cut the cord between them or forget his pledge. He keeps faith though she has broken it.

translation: Has the night been changed, so that its stars do not move,
or has it grown so long I think the Pleiades have lost their way?
34.sharh: Either the night has changed and its stars no longer travel, or it is so long that the Pleiades seem to have lost their way. The lover lies awake, and the night will not end.

translation: Many a woman in the Ghawr who visits the sick, had she seen,
would grieve at our complaint at Dayr al-Lujj.
35.sharh: He lies ill far away, perhaps of love, with no one by him to visit and pity him; shakwa, “complaint”, is also illness.

translation: The eyes whose glance is deep black set in white
have killed us, and never brought their dead to life again.
36.sharh: Love's victims stay dead. It is one of the most quoted love lines in Arabic, and Ibn Qutayba quotes it.

translation: They fell the man of sense until he cannot stir,
and they are the frailest-built of God's creatures.
37.sharh: These eyes throw down the man of sense until he cannot move, though they belong to the frailest of God's creatures. The paradox is the point: the weakest overcome the strongest minds.

translation: Many who envy us, if they sought you,
would meet with distance from you, and denial.
38.sharh: Many envy the poet his place near her; if they sought her themselves, they would meet with nothing but distance and refusal. Others envy him a nearness he does not have, and the next line says what it would cost them.

translation: They have shown him death, until there is no life in him;
they had dealt with you in the same ways before.
39.sharh: The eyes have shown the envious man death until no life is left in him; and they had treated the poet the same way long before. What the envious would suffer, he has already suffered.

translation: My heart flew off with the soft young woman who came
by night in my sleep, sweet-scented in every curve, full-bodied,
40.sharh: The beloved's phantom visiting the lover in sleep is a favourite theme of the old poets.

translation: her mouth cool after sleep, uncovering
coiled tresses that drip with musk and ben-oil.
41.sharh: A cool mouth on waking was a sign of sweet breath, and her hair is perfumed.

translation: We passed the night seeing ourselves as if we were our own masters:
if only our dream had come true.
42.sharh: All night in the dream they were their own masters, with no one to keep them apart; if only the dream had come true. Sleep gives what waking life denies.

translation: She said, “Be patient: our people have set
doors and guards between us and any visit.”
43.sharh: She tells him to bear it: her people have put doors and guards between them. Her tribe keeps her under watch, and the freedom of the dream cannot come true.

translation: When I saw that they were barred from us,
armies like death came over me.
44.sharh: When he saw that the way to them was barred, sorrows came down on him like armies, each as overwhelming as death.

translation: What I suffered from the litters on the day of Qana,
following a man who goes far from home, forever moving on and parting.
45.sharh: The litters follow a man who goes far from home and is always moving on: the parting is his doing.

translation: I followed them with an eye whose pupil was drowned:
will this, I wonder, leave the eye its pupil?
46.sharh: He fears his tears will wash his eye away. The editions read “will what you see”; the reciter says “will this, I wonder”.

translation: Their litters, driven off with songs, looked
like palms at Malham, or palms at Qurran.
47.sharh: As the litters were driven off to the drivers' songs, they looked from far off like the palm groves of Malham or Qurran. Tall litters swaying in a line on a distant road look like rows of palms.

translation: Umm Uthman, what our camels go through.
Just measure our morning halt from our evening halt.
48.sharh: Umm Uthman should measure the ground between their morning halt and their evening halt to know what the camels suffer. A single day's march covers a great distance.

translation: Noble camels speed with us, their footpads bloodied
by running over rough rises, stony ground after stony ground.
49.sharh: Noble camels carry them at speed, and the rough stony uplands, one after another, have bloodied their footpads. The road is as hard on the camels as love is on the rider.

translation: They cast their eyes towards Najd, having crossed
the cairns between al-Salawtah and al-Rawhan.
50.sharh: Having crossed the cairns between al-Salawtah and al-Rawhan, the camels keep turning their eyes towards Najd. They long for home as their riders do.

translation: How dear a mountain is Mount al-Rayyan,
and dear whoever lives on al-Rayyan.
51.sharh: Mount al-Rayyan is dear, and dear whoever lives there, whoever that may be. He loves the mountain, and everyone on it, for the sake of the one who lived near it.

translation: And dear the breaths of the south wind
that come to you at times from the side of al-Rayyan.
52.sharh: Dear too are the gusts of the south wind that blow at times from the side of al-Rayyan. The wind comes from her country, and brings her to mind.

translation: It blew from the north, and I remembered you
by the smooth rock east of Hawran.
53.sharh: When the north wind blew he remembered them, by the smooth rock east of Hawran. Far away in Syria, he remembers her with every wind, from the south or the north.

translation: Will it ever come back, though time brings nothing back,
the life there that was so sweet and gentle,
54.sharh: He asks whether the sweet, easy life he once had there will ever return, though time gives nothing back. He asks, knowing the answer.

translation: the days when they called me Satan for my love-talk,
and loved me when I was a Satan?
55.sharh: In his youth the women called him a devil for his flirting, and loved him for it.

translation: Whoever seethes with rage that I visit you,
the King of mankind has grown angry with him.
56.sharh: Here the love prelude ends and the threats begin. The King of mankind is God, or perhaps the caliph: the poet is in Syria (line 53).

translation: What are the poets of the land stalking, woe to them?
The pounce of the lion that lurks in his thicket at Khaffan.
57.sharh: The poets are hunters creeping up on a lion; they do not see that the game will spring on them.

translation: In folly and error they wished I would drive them with my song:
I have driven them, two at a time and one by one.
58.sharh: The poets foolishly wished he would drive them with his song, and he has driven them, in pairs and one by one. Huda', the camel-driver's song, is his satire: they wanted his attention, and they got it.

translation: I left them, some worn out and dead on the yoking rope,
and others who forgot how to roar, like gelded camels.
59.sharh: Some of his rivals are finished; others have fallen silent, like stallions that no longer bellow.

translation: My twisted rope stayed round their necks
until my rage was quenched, and whoever would submit submitted.
60.sharh: His twisted rope stayed round their necks until his anger was satisfied and whoever would submit had submitted. He leads his rivals like captured camels on the rope of his satire.

translation: Whoever of them calls me out, seeking war with me,
let him be sure I will answer him wide awake.
61.sharh: Any of them who calls him out to fight in verse can be sure he will answer at once, wide awake: wasnan is the drowsy man caught half asleep, and he will never be taken unawares.

translation: My tooth never bites a people until I have told them:
“Beware, and again beware, and beware of us.”
62.sharh: He never bites a people with his satire before warning them: beware, and again beware of us. He always warns before he bites, so no one is caught unawares.

translation: I am a man who has never meant, against those I contend with,
to wrong anyone, nor to fawn in war.
63.sharh: In his quarrels he has never meant to wrong anyone, nor has he ever made a show of peace in war. He fights openly and fairly: idhan is the soft word that hides hostility, and he will have none of it.

translation: I guard my preserve, by my high place in glory
among Khindif, and the heights of Qays Aylan.
64.sharh: Khindif and Qays Aylan are the two great branches of Mudar: he is of Khindif through Tamim, and claims the heights of Qays as well. The reciter says this line twice.

1.1.2.meaning: Al-khalit: those who camp with one, the neighbouring families of the beloved.

1.2.5.head: قَرَن
1.2.5.meaning: Aqran: ropes that tie one camel to another.

3.1.5.head: ظَعينَة
3.1.5.meaning: Az'an: the departing camels with their women in litters.

3.1.7.meaning: Tarab: a sudden stirring of the heart, by grief or joy.

10.1.1.head: أَهدى
10.1.1.meaning: Tuhdi: you bring, addressed to the rider. Both editions have nuhdi, “we send”.

10.1.6.meaning: Malah: a watering place of the Banu al-Adawiyya.

11.1.4.meaning: Jiz': the bend of a valley.

11.2.3.head: عَطَن
11.2.3.meaning: A'tan: the pens round a well where camels kneel.

12.2.5.meaning: Sulwan: forgetting; also a stone the Arabs dipped in water for a lover to drink and forget.

14.2.5.meaning: Dajn: a day of cloud and rain.

16.1.2.meaning: Tayba: the beloved's name, shortened in the vocative.

19.2.6.meaning: Insan: a person, and the pupil of the eye.

20.1.2.head: غَريم
20.1.2.meaning: Gharim: one who has a claim, a creditor.

24.2.4.head: بَيدان
24.2.4.meaning: Baydan: a watering place of the Banu Ja'far.

25.1.3-4.meaning: Liwa Hawwa': liwa is the edge of a sand tract; Hawwa' a watering place in al-Yamama.

25.2.6.meaning: Qurhan: one untouched by something; properly, one who has never had smallpox or been wounded in war.

27.2.2.head: أَمير
27.2.2.meaning: Amir: here, the man in charge of her, her guardian.

30.1.5.meaning: Shara': open to all who come to drink.

31.1.5.head: مَحضَر
31.1.5.meaning: Mahdar: the summer camp by the wells.

31.2.4.head: مَبدى
31.2.4.meaning: Mabda: the spring camp out in the open desert.

32.1.3.meaning: Al-Irq: a valley of the Banu Hanzala.

32.2.4.head: السُّلّان
32.2.4.meaning: Al-Sullan: a valley of the Banu Amr ibn Tamim.

34.2.6.head: حَيران
34.2.6.meaning: Hayran: “bewildered”, unable to find its way.

35.2.3-4.meaning: Dayr al-Lujj: a monastery near al-Hira, in Iraq.

36.1.6.meaning: Hawar: eyes with a vivid white around a deep black. Both editions have marad, “languor”.

37.1.6.meaning: Harak: movement. Both editions have sira', “strength to wrestle”.

39.2.3.head: دانَ
39.2.3.meaning: Dinna-ka: they have made it your habit, they have treated you so; din is a habitual way of dealing. The poet is speaking to himself.

40.1.4.meaning: Khawd: a soft, graceful young woman.

41.2.3.meaning: Mathan: coiled tresses, braids folded over one another.

41.2.6.head: البان
41.2.6.meaning: Ban: the ben tree, whose oil was used as perfume.

47.1.2.head: حِدج
47.1.2.meaning: Ahdaj: women's litters carried on camels.

49.1.5.head: مَنسِم
49.1.5.meaning: Manasim: the tips of a camel's footpads.

49.2.2.head: حِزباءَة
49.2.2.meaning: Hazabi: rough rises in the ground.

50.2.2.meaning: Al-Salawtah: a place in the Jazira, upper Mesopotamia.

50.2.3.head: الرَّوحان
50.2.3.meaning: Al-Rawhan: the farthest lands of the Banu Sa'd.

50.2.4.head: صُوَّة
50.2.4.meaning: Suwwan: stone cairns that mark the way.

51.1.4.meaning: Al-Rayyan: a mountain of the Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'a.

52.1.4.head: يَمانِيَة
52.1.4.meaning: Yamaniya: the south wind, blowing from the Yemen.

53.2.5.meaning: Hawran: a district south of Damascus.

57.1.2.head: اِدَّرى
57.1.2.meaning: Yaddari: stalks, lies in wait for game.

57.2.3.head: مُخدِر
57.2.3.meaning: Mukhdir: a lion lurking in its thicket.

57.2.5.head: خَفّان
57.2.5.meaning: Khaffan: a place on the road to Kufa known for its lions.

58.1.3.head: حُداء
58.1.3.meaning: Huda': the song with which camels are driven.

59.1.6.meaning: Qaran: the rope that yokes two camels together.

59.2.3.meaning: Tahdar: the roaring of a stallion camel.

62.1.3.head: ناب
62.1.3.meaning: Nab: canine tooth; his bite is his satire.

64.2.2.meaning: Khindif: the wife of Ilyas ibn Mudar, from whom Tamim, Asad, Quraysh and other tribes descend.

64.2.5-6.meaning: Qays Aylan: the other great branch of Mudar, ancestor of Hawazin, Sulaym and Ghatafan.
